claim: The study measured mRNA profiles in 15 yeast species from the phylum Ascomycota.
source: Here, we used a phylogenetic framework to measure mRNA profiles in 15 yeast species from the phylum Ascomycota and reconstruct the evolution of their modular regulatory programs along a time course of growth on glucose over 300 million years.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the number of species and their taxonomic classification.

claim: The study reconstructed the evolution of modular regulatory programs over 300 million years.
source: Here, we used a phylogenetic framework to measure mRNA profiles in 15 yeast species from the phylum Ascomycota and reconstruct the evolution of their modular regulatory programs along a time course of growth on glucose over 300 million years.
evidence: The abstract states the temporal span of evolutionary reconstruction.

claim: Modules have diverged proportionally to phylogenetic distance.
source: We found that modules have diverged proportionally to phylogenetic distance, with prominent changes in gene regulation accompanying changes in lifestyle and ploidy, especially in carbon metabolism.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding about module divergence.

claim: Prominent changes in gene regulation accompany changes in lifestyle and ploidy, especially in carbon metabolism.
source: We found that modules have diverged proportionally to phylogenetic distance, with prominent changes in gene regulation accompanying changes in lifestyle and ploidy, especially in carbon metabolism.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this association between regulatory changes and phenotypic changes.

claim: The mechanisms through which regulatory systems evolve are still only partially understood.
source: However, the mechanisms through which regulatory systems evolve are still only partially understood, and in most cases the adaptive importance of regulatory changes is unknown (Lynch, 2007; Thompson and Regev, 2009; Wohlbach et al., 2009; Baker et al., 2012; Romero et al., 2012).
evidence: The introduction states this as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Comparative genomics approaches have allowed tracing the evolution of gene regulation at different time scales.
source: In recent years, comparative genomics approaches have allowed us to begin to trace the evolution of gene regulation at different time scales (Tuch et al., 2008b; Weirauch and Hughes, 2010; Brawand et al., 2011; Lindblad-Toh et al., 2011; Romero et al., 2012), through two major approaches: (1) characterization of cis-regulatory elements in orthologous promoter sequences (Gasch et al., 2004; Tanay et al., 2005; Bradley et al., 2010; Lindblad-Toh et al., 2011; Habib et al., 2012), and (2) comparative analysis of mRNA profiles and protein–DNA interactions measured across organisms (Tirosh et al., 2006, 2011; Borneman et al., 2007; Tuch et al., 2008a; Schmidt et al., 2010; Wapinski et al., 2010; Brawand et al., 2011; Romero et al., 2012).
evidence: The introduction cites prior work on comparative genomics approaches.

claim: One major approach to trace evolution of gene regulation is characterization of cis-regulatory elements in orthologous promoter sequences.
source: In recent years, comparative genomics approaches have allowed us to begin to trace the evolution of gene regulation at different time scales (Tuch et al., 2008b; Weirauch and Hughes, 2010; Brawand et al., 2011; Lindblad-Toh et al., 2011; Romero et al., 2012), through two major approaches: (1) characterization of cis-regulatory elements in orthologous promoter sequences (Gasch et al., 2004; Tanay et al., 2005; Bradley et al., 2010; Lindblad-Toh et al., 2011; Habib et al., 2012), and (2) comparative analysis of mRNA profiles and protein–DNA interactions measured across organisms (Tirosh et al., 2006, 2011; Borneman et al., 2007; Tuch et al., 2008a; Schmidt et al., 2010; Wapinski et al., 2010; Brawand et al., 2011; Romero et al., 2012).
evidence: The introduction describes this as one of two major approaches.

claim: Another major approach to trace evolution of gene regulation is comparative analysis of mRNA profiles and protein–DNA interactions measured across organisms.
source: In recent years, comparative genomics approaches have allowed us to begin to trace the evolution of gene regulation at different time scales (Tuch et al., 2008b; Weirauch and Hughes, 2010; Brawand et al., 2011; Lindblad-Toh et al., 2011; Romero et al., 2012), through two major approaches: (1) characterization of cis-regulatory elements in orthologous promoter sequences (Gasch et al., 2004; Tanay et al., 2005; Bradley et al., 2010; Lindblad-Toh et al., 2011; Habib et al., 2012), and (2) comparative analysis of mRNA profiles and protein–DNA interactions measured across organisms (Tirosh et al., 2006, 2011; Borneman et al., 2007; Tuch et al., 2008a; Schmidt et al., 2010; Wapinski et al., 2010; Brawand et al., 2011; Romero et al., 2012).
evidence: The introduction describes this as one of two major approaches.

claim: Studies relying on cis-regulatory sequences are more prevalent than functional studies.
source: While studies relying on cis-regulatory sequences are more prevalent, functional studies of comparative gene regulation are beginning to shed light on how regulatory evolution is linked to functional changes.
evidence: The introduction compares the prevalence of different approaches.

claim: Gene duplication can promote regulatory divergence by neo-functionalization or sub-functionalization of regulatory mechanisms of the two paralogs.
source: In particular, it has been suggested (Lynch and Force, 2000; Gu et al., 2004, 2005; Teichmann and Babu, 2004; ; Conant and Wolfe, 2006; Tirosh and Barkai, 2007; Wapinski et al., 2007b) that gene duplication can promote regulatory divergence by either neo-functionalization or sub-functionalization of regulatory mechanisms of the two paralogs.
evidence: The introduction cites prior theoretical work on gene duplication and regulatory divergence.

claim: The Ascomycota fungi provide an excellent model to study the evolution of gene regulation.
source: Among eukaryotes, the Ascomycota fungi (Figure 1A) provide an excellent model to study the evolution of gene regulation (Tsong et al., 2003, 2006; Ihmels et al., 2005; Tanay et al., 2005; Field et al., 2008; Hogues et al., 2008; Tirosh and Barkai, 2008; Tsankov et al., 2010, 2011; Baker et al., 2012; Habib et al., 2012).
evidence: The introduction states this and cites prior work using this system.

claim: Ascomycota include the model organisms Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Schizosaccharomyces pombe and Candida albicans.
source: They include the model organisms Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Schizosaccharomyces pombe and Candida albicans, as well as many non-model, genetically-tractable species with sequenced genomes.
evidence: The introduction lists these as model organisms within Ascomycota.

claim: Species in the Ascomycota phylogeny diverged before and after a whole genome duplication event.
source: Species in the phylogeny diverged before and after a whole genome duplication event (Wolfe and Shields, 1997; Kellis et al., 2004) (WGD, Figure 1A, star, ∼150 mya), allowing us to study the consequences of this evolutionary mechanism (Wolfe and Shields, 1997; Kellis et al., 2004; Wapinski et al., 2007b).
evidence: The introduction states this and cites prior work on the WGD event.

claim: The whole genome duplication event occurred approximately 150 million years ago.
source: Species in the phylogeny diverged before and after a whole genome duplication event (Wolfe and Shields, 1997; Kellis et al., 2004) (WGD, Figure 1A, star, ∼150 mya), allowing us to study the consequences of this evolutionary mechanism (Wolfe and Shields, 1997; Kellis et al., 2004; Wapinski et al., 2007b).
evidence: The introduction provides a temporal estimate for the WGD event.

claim: Co-expression of genes in modules can be conserved at substantial distances in yeast.
source: For example, studies in yeast showed that while co-expression of genes in modules can be conserved at substantial distances, the associated regulatory mechanisms often diverge, acquiring new regulators and losing ancestral ones, both for sequence-specific transcription factors (Tsong et al., 2003, 2006; Tanay et al., 2005; Hogues et al., 2008; Lavoie et al., 2010; Baker et al., 2011, 2012) and for chromatin organization (Tirosh and Barkai, 2008; Tsankov et al., 2010, 2011).
evidence: The introduction cites prior work on conservation of co-expression.

claim: The regulatory mechanisms associated with co-expressed modules often diverge, acquiring new regulators and losing ancestral ones.
source: For example, studies in yeast showed that while co-expression of genes in modules can be conserved at substantial distances, the associated regulatory mechanisms often diverge, acquiring new regulators and losing ancestral ones, both for sequence-specific transcription factors (Tsong et al., 2003, 2006; Tanay et al., 2005; Hogues et al., 2008; Lavoie et al., 2010; Baker et al., 2011, 2012) and for chromatin organization (Tirosh and Barkai, 2008; Tsankov et al., 2010, 2011).
evidence: The introduction cites prior work on divergence of regulatory mechanisms.

claim: In some cases, changes in gene expression and related mechanisms are clearly coupled to other adaptive changes in lifestyle.
source: In some cases, changes in gene expression and related mechanisms are clearly coupled to other adaptive changes in lifestyle (Ihmels et al., 2005; Field et al., 2008; Tsankov et al., 2010), whereas in others they may be the result of neutral 'regulatory drift' (Tsong et al., 2003, 2006; Lavoie et al., 2010; Baker et al., 2012).
evidence: The introduction cites prior work on adaptive changes in gene expression.

claim: In some cases, changes in gene expression may be the result of neutral 'regulatory drift'.
source: In some cases, changes in gene expression and related mechanisms are clearly coupled to other adaptive changes in lifestyle (Ihmels et al., 2005; Field et al., 2008; Tsankov et al., 2010), whereas in others they may be the result of neutral 'regulatory drift' (Tsong et al., 2003, 2006; Lavoie et al., 2010; Baker et al., 2012).
evidence: The introduction cites prior work on neutral regulatory drift.

claim: Most experimental studies rely on two to four species.
source: Despite these early successes, collecting experimental data across species has remained challenging, and hence most experimental studies rely on two to four species (Tanay et al., 2005; Tirosh et al., 2006; Lelandais et al., 2008; Wittkopp et al., 2008), with few exceptions (Schmidt et al., 2010; Tsankov et al., 2010; Wapinski et al., 2010; Brawand et al., 2011; He et al., 2011).
evidence: The introduction cites prior work and notes the typical number of species studied.

claim: The 15 species studied span >300 million years of evolution.
source: Here, we use comparative transcriptional studies across 15 Ascomycota species—spanning >300 million years of evolution (Sipiczki, 2000)—to understand the evolution of modular gene regulation during batch growth on glucose and its depletion, a key physiological response.
evidence: The introduction states the temporal span of the species studied.

claim: The study collected approximately 300 expression profiles at six physiologically comparable time points along each species' growth.
source: We optimized culture conditions across species, and collected ∼300 expression profiles at six physiologically comparable time points along each species' growth: repletion (lag phase), exponential growth ('mid-log' and 'late log'), the point of glucose depletion ('diauxic shift') and two later time points when the growth rate levels off ('post shift' and 'plateau').
evidence: The introduction describes the experimental design and number of profiles collected.

claim: The six time points sampled were repletion (lag phase), exponential growth ('mid-log' and 'late log'), the point of glucose depletion ('diauxic shift') and two later time points when the growth rate levels off ('post shift' and 'plateau').
source: We optimized culture conditions across species, and collected ∼300 expression profiles at six physiologically comparable time points along each species' growth: repletion (lag phase), exponential growth ('mid-log' and 'late log'), the point of glucose depletion ('diauxic shift') and two later time points when the growth rate levels off ('post shift' and 'plateau').
evidence: The introduction describes the time points sampled.

claim: Arboretum is a new algorithm used to identify expression modules across species and to reconstruct their evolutionary history.
source: To analyze the evolution of regulatory modules, we use a new algorithm, Arboretum (Roy et al., 2013), to identify expression modules across species and to reconstruct their evolutionary history.
evidence: The introduction describes the computational method used.

claim: The degree of divergence of the transcriptional profiles correlates with phylogenetic distance.
source: We find that the degree of divergence of the transcriptional profiles correlates with phylogenetic distance, with the largest divergence in lag phase profiles.
evidence: The introduction summarizes a key finding of the study.

claim: The largest divergence in transcriptional profiles occurs in lag phase profiles.
source: We find that the degree of divergence of the transcriptional profiles correlates with phylogenetic distance, with the largest divergence in lag phase profiles.

source: In all species, the transcriptional response involves five major transcriptional modules.

claim: Module gene membership diverges proportionally to phylogenetic distance.
source: While the module's expression patterns are conserved across species, their gene membership diverges, proportionally to phylogenetic distance.

claim: Gene duplication events significantly contribute to regulatory divergence, in particular close to their phylogenetic point of duplication.
source: Gene duplication events significantly contribute to regulatory divergence, in particular close to their phylogenetic point of duplication.

claim: The contribution of gene duplication to regulatory divergence is more pronounced and more prolonged for WGD paralogs.
source: This contribution is more pronounced and more prolonged for WGD paralogs.

claim: The patterns observed in glucose depletion also characterize the evolution of the transcriptional response to heat shock.
source: These patterns also characterize the evolution of the transcriptional response to heat shock, supporting their generality (Roy et al., 2013).
evidence: The introduction summarizes a key finding about generality of patterns.

claim: The framework for comparative functional genomics is applicable to any complex phylogeny.

source: Species in the Kluyveromyces, Candida, and Yarrowia clades are respiratory and use oxidative phosphorylation (Figure 1A, red and green).
evidence: The results section describes the carbon metabolism phenotypes of different clades.

claim: A respiro-fermentative lifestyle has evolved independently at least twice in the Ascomycota phylogeny.
source: Conversely, a respiro-fermentative lifestyle—a preference to ferment glucose even in the presence of oxygen (Piskur et al., 2006)—has evolved independently at least twice in this phylogeny, once after the WGD (Conant and Wolfe, 2007) and once in Schizosaccharomyces (Rhind et al., 2011) (Figure 1A, dark blue).
evidence: The results section describes the evolution of respiro-fermentation.

claim: Respiro-fermentation evolved once after the WGD.

claim: Y. lipolytica is an obligate respiratory species.
source: In contrast to the other respiratory species that can ferment, Y. lipolytica (Figure 1A, green) is an obligate respiratory species, but can uniquely use normal hydrocarbons and various fats as carbon sources (Kurtzman, 2000).

claim: The degree of correlation in expression profiles is inversely related with the phylogenetic distance between species.
source: We found that the degree of correlation is inversely related with the phylogenetic distance between the species (r<−0.39 to −0.77, p<3 × 10−5, Figure 3B–F), such that the closer two species are in the phylogeny, the higher the correlation between their profiles.
evidence: The results section states this finding with statistical support and reference to figures.

claim: The closer two species are in the phylogeny, the higher the correlation between their expression profiles.
source: We found that the degree of correlation is inversely related with the phylogenetic distance between the species (r<−0.39 to −0.77, p<3 × 10−5, Figure 3B–F), such that the closer two species are in the phylogeny, the higher the correlation between their profiles.
evidence: The results section states this finding with statistical support.

claim: This inverse relation between phylogenetic distance and expression correlation is apparent at each of the time points.
source: This inverse relation is apparent at each of the time points (Figure 3B–F), and is consistent with what was recently reported in mammals (Brawand et al., 2011).
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figures.

claim: The inverse relation between phylogenetic distance and expression correlation is consistent with what was recently reported in mammals.
source: This inverse relation is apparent at each of the time points (Figure 3B–F), and is consistent with what was recently reported in mammals (Brawand et al., 2011).
evidence: The results section compares the finding to prior work in mammals.

claim: Profiles at diauxic shift, post shift and plateau are the most correlated between species.
source: Profiles at diauxic shift, post shift and plateau are the most correlated between species (Figure 3D–G), whereas the lag profiles, when cells 'reset' in response to nutrient repletion, are the most divergent (Figure 3B,G), likely reflecting species-specific responses to nutrient signals shaped by niche adaptation.
evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figures.

claim: The lag profiles are the most divergent between species.

evidence: The results section states this finding with reference to figures.

claim: The divergence of lag profiles likely reflects species-specific responses to nutrient signals shaped by niche adaptation.

evidence: The results section interprets the lag phase divergence.

claim: S. japonicus and S. castellii were the most divergent species.
source: S. japonicus and S. castellii were the most divergent, such that in some cases, their Lag phase profiles were even anti-correlated to those of other species, suggesting distinct repletion programs.

claim: Arboretum uses the structures of gene trees during module identification.

evidence: The results section states this finding with statistical support.

claim: Genes assigned in the LCA to Module 1 tend to persist in that module (Module Stability 94% ± 0.5%).
source: Genes assigned in the LCA to Modules 1 (Figure 4B, blue entries) and 5 (Figure 4F, red entries) tend to persist in those modules (Module Stability 94% ± 0.5% and 84% ± 1.2%, respectively, 'Materials and methods').
evidence: The results section reports the module stability for Module 1.

claim: Genes assigned in the LCA to Module 5 tend to persist in that module (Module Stability 84% ± 1.2%).
source: Genes assigned in the LCA to Modules 1 (Figure 4B, blue entries) and 5 (Figure 4F, red entries) tend to persist in those modules (Module Stability 94% ± 0.5% and 84% ± 1.2%, respectively, 'Materials and methods').
evidence: The results section reports the module stability for Module 5.

claim: Modules 2, 3, and 4 are less stable, with more frequent reassignment of their member genes to other modules.
source: Conversely, Modules 2, 3, and 4 (Figure 4C–E) are less stable, with more frequent reassignment of their member genes to other modules.
evidence: The results section compares the stability of different modules.

claim: Module 1 and 5 are the least dynamic as reflected by the average proportion of genes that join (11% ± 1.6% and 17% ± 1.7%, respectively) or leave each module (6% ± 0.4% and 16% ± 1%, respectively).
source: Module 1 and 5 are the least dynamic as reflected by the average proportion of genes that join (11% ± 1.6% and 17% ± 1.7%, respectively) or leave each module (6% ± 0.4% and 16% ± 1%, respectively) between each pair of ancestor and child species in the phylogeny (Module Expansion Index and Module Contraction Index, respectively, 'Materials and methods'; Figure 5D,E).
evidence: The results section reports the module expansion and contraction indices.

claim: Cell cycle and DNA replication genes are reassigned in a coordinated fashion from Module 3 in the LCA to Modules 4 and 5 in Schizosaccharomyces.
source: For example, cell cycle and DNA replication genes are reassigned in a coordinated fashion from Module 3 in the LCA to Modules 4 and 5 in Schizosaccharomyces (Figure 6A), consistent with the unique nutrient control of mating in this clade (Nadin-Davis and Nasim, 1990).
evidence: The results section describes a specific example of coordinated reassignment.

claim: The reassignment of cell cycle and DNA replication genes in Schizosaccharomyces is consistent with the unique nutrient control of mating in this clade.
source: For example, cell cycle and DNA replication genes are reassigned in a coordinated fashion from Module 3 in the LCA to Modules 4 and 5 in Schizosaccharomyces (Figure 6A), consistent with the unique nutrient control of mating in this clade (Nadin-Davis and Nasim, 1990).
evidence: The results section interprets the reassignment in the context of known biology.

claim: Ploidy- and meiosis-related genes are reassigned from the strongly induced Module 5 in the typically haploid pre-WGD species to the unchanged Module 3 or repressed Module 2 in the typically diploid post-WGD species.
source: In another case, both ploidy- and meiosis-related genes (Figure 6B) are reassigned from the strongly induced Module 5 in the typically haploid pre-WGD species to the unchanged Module 3 or repressed Module 2 in the typically diploid post-WGD species.
evidence: The results section describes another example of coordinated reassignment.

claim: The reassignment of ploidy- and meiosis-related genes is likely due to shifts in nutrient control of mating and meiosis post-WGD.
source: This is likely due to shifts in nutrient control of mating and meiosis post-WGD (Barsoum et al., 2011).
evidence: The results section interprets the reassignment in the context of known biology.

claim: Arboretum infers that the LCA (A14) followed the haploid, Module 5, pattern for ploidy- and meiosis-related genes.
source: Arboretum infers that the LCA (A14) followed the haploid, Module 5, pattern (Figure 6B, middle panel, A14 column).
evidence: The results section states the ancestral state inferred by Arboretum.

claim: The reassignment of mitochondrial genes is consistent with previous hypotheses that respiro-fermentation is the derived state.
source: This is consistent with previous hypotheses that respiro-fermentation is the derived state (Piskur et al., 2006).
evidence: The results section interprets the reassignment in the context of prior hypotheses.

claim: Oxidative phosphorylation genes show a gradual shift from repression in Y. lipolytica to late induction in Kluyveromyces to strong induction post-WGD.
source: Similar changes have occurred in the expression of oxidative phosphorylation genes (Figure 6D), albeit with a more gradual shift from repression in Y. lipolytica to late induction in Kluyveromyces to strong induction post-WGD (Figure 6D, left panel).
evidence: The results section describes the expression pattern of oxidative phosphorylation genes.

claim: Changes in oxidative phosphorylation gene expression are associated with concomitant changes in nucleosome organization and anti nucleosomal polydA:dT sequences in the promoters of oxidative phosphorylation and mRP genes.
source: This is associated with concomitant changes in nucleosome organization and anti nucleosomal polydA:dT sequences in the promoters of oxidative phosphorylation and mRP genes (Field et al., 2008; Tsankov et al., 2010), which occurred convergently post-WGD and in Schizosaccharomyces (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: The results section describes associated changes in chromatin organization.

claim: Changes in nucleosome organization occurred convergently post-WGD and in Schizosaccharomyces.
source: This is associated with concomitant changes in nucleosome organization and anti nucleosomal polydA:dT sequences in the promoters of oxidative phosphorylation and mRP genes (Field et al., 2008; Tsankov et al., 2010), which occurred convergently post-WGD and in Schizosaccharomyces (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: The results section describes the convergent evolution of chromatin changes.

claim: The promoters of mRP and respiration genes have lost the binding site for the transcription factor Sfp1 in many respirofermentative species.
source: In addition, the promoters of mRP and respiration genes have lost the binding site for the transcription factor Sfp1 (previously identified as the 'Rapid Growth Element', RGE; Ihmels et al., 2005) in many respirofermentative species (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The results section describes the loss of Sfp1 binding sites.

claim: The Sfp1 binding site is strongly conserved in 'growth' (Module 1) genes across all species (except S. japonicus).
source: The Sfp1 binding site is strongly conserved in 'growth' (Module 1) genes across all species (except S. japonicus) and serves as an ancient regulatory tether of the growth module (p<0.05, Hyper-geometric test; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The results section describes the conservation of Sfp1 binding sites in growth genes.

claim: The Sfp1 binding site serves as an ancient regulatory tether of the growth module.
source: The Sfp1 binding site is strongly conserved in 'growth' (Module 1) genes across all species (except S. japonicus) and serves as an ancient regulatory tether of the growth module (p<0.05, Hyper-geometric test; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The results section interprets the conservation of Sfp1 binding sites.

claim: The Sfp1 binding site was lost from mRP gene promoters in post-WGD species and S. japonicus.
source: This site was lost from mRP gene promoters in post-WGD species (Ihmels et al., 2005; Tanay et al., 2005) and S. japonicus (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The results section describes the loss of Sfp1 binding sites from mRP genes.

claim: In S. pombe and K. polysporus some mRP genes have lost the Sfp1 site whereas others retain it.
source: In S. pombe and K. polysporus some genes have lost the site whereas others retain it, where the number retained is an intermediate between that in post-WGD species and in respiratory species (Jiang et al., 2008).
evidence: The results section describes the intermediate state of Sfp1 site retention in these species.

claim: The Sfp1 motif is enriched in oxidative phosphorylation gene promoters in some of the respiratory species.
source: The Sfp1 motif is also enriched in oxidative phosphorylation gene promoters in some of the respiratory species (Hyper-geometric, p<0.05, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The results section describes the enrichment of Sfp1 motif in oxidative phosphorylation genes.

claim: Purine metabolism and amino acid catabolism genes in pathways that feed nucleotide synthesis are reassigned from mildly repressed or unchanged Modules 2 and 3 pre-WGD to the strongly induced Module 5 post-WGD.
source: Indeed, more surprisingly, purine metabolism and amino acid catabolism genes in pathways that feed nucleotide synthesis (Figure 8A) are reassigned from mildly repressed or unchanged Modules 2 and 3 pre-WGD to the strongly induced Module 5 post-WGD (Figure 6E).
evidence: The results section describes the reassignment of purine and amino acid metabolism genes.

claim: The regulatory changes in purine metabolism and amino acid catabolism genes were not previously recognized.
source: These regulatory changes were not previously recognized, to the best of our knowledge, and are reminiscent of those observed in the Warburg effect (Vander Heiden et al., 2009), a cancer metabolic state analogous to respiro-fermentation (see 'Discussion'), including the induction of the glycine biosynthetic pathway that was recently shown to be correlated with proliferation rates across different cancers (Jain et al., 2012).
evidence: The results section states that these changes are novel findings.

claim: The regulatory changes in purine metabolism and amino acid catabolism genes are reminiscent of those observed in the Warburg effect.
source: These regulatory changes were not previously recognized, to the best of our knowledge, and are reminiscent of those observed in the Warburg effect (Vander Heiden et al., 2009), a cancer metabolic state analogous to respiro-fermentation (see 'Discussion'), including the induction of the glycine biosynthetic pathway that was recently shown to be correlated with proliferation rates across different cancers (Jain et al., 2012).
evidence: The results section draws an analogy to the Warburg effect.

claim: The Warburg effect is a cancer metabolic state analogous to respiro-fermentation.
source: These regulatory changes were not previously recognized, to the best of our knowledge, and are reminiscent of those observed in the Warburg effect (Vander Heiden et al., 2009), a cancer metabolic state analogous to respiro-fermentation (see 'Discussion'), including the induction of the glycine biosynthetic pathway that was recently shown to be correlated with proliferation rates across different cancers (Jain et al., 2012).
evidence: The results section states this analogy.

claim: The induction of the glycine biosynthetic pathway was recently shown to be correlated with proliferation rates across different cancers.
source: These regulatory changes were not previously recognized, to the best of our knowledge, and are reminiscent of those observed in the Warburg effect (Vander Heiden et al., 2009), a cancer metabolic state analogous to respiro-fermentation (see 'Discussion'), including the induction of the glycine biosynthetic pathway that was recently shown to be correlated with proliferation rates across different cancers (Jain et al., 2012).
evidence: The results section cites prior work on glycine biosynthesis in cancer.

claim: The re-assignment of purine metabolism and amino acid catabolism genes is unique to the post-WGD species and does not occur in Schizosacchromyces.
source: Unlike mRP and oxidative phosphorylation genes, this re-assignment is unique to the post-WGD species and does not occur in Schizosacchromyces (Figure 6E).
evidence: The results section contrasts this reassignment with that of other genes.

claim: The re-assignment of purine metabolism and amino acid catabolism genes is associated with the shifting of binding sites for key activators from nucleosome-free to nucleosome-occluded positions in rich media post-WGD.
source: It is associated with the shifting of binding sites for key activators of amino acid and purine biosynthesis genes (e.g., Bas1, Met32, Gzf3, Gln3, Met28, Met4, and Gat1) from nucleosome-free to nucleosome-occluded positions (Tsankov et al., 2010) in rich media post-WGD (Figure 7C).
evidence: The results section describes associated changes in nucleosome positioning.

claim: Genes that have a paralog were more likely to change their module assignment than those present in a single copy.
source: Genes that have a paralog were more likely to change their module assignment than those present in a single copy (KS test, p<1.5 × 10−107).
evidence: The results section states this finding with statistical support.

claim: Paralogous genes are much more likely to be reassigned after duplication than their corresponding pre-duplication orthologs.
source: Furthermore, controlling for any differences in function between duplicated and non-duplicated genes, paralogous genes are much more likely to be reassigned after duplication than their corresponding pre-duplication orthologs (Figure 10D,E, KS test, p<1 × 10−18).
evidence: The results section states this finding with statistical support.

claim: The increased divergence of paralogs was most prominent at the WGD ancestor (A5) and the Schizosaccharomyces ancestor (A13).
source: This increased divergence was most prominent at the WGD ancestor (A5) and the Schizosaccharomyces ancestor (A13) (Figure 10A).
evidence: The results section identifies the phylogenetic points with most divergence.

claim: The WGD ancestor and Schizosaccharomyces ancestor have a larger number of retained paralog pairs compared to other ancestral species.
source: Both ancestors also have a larger number of retained paralog pairs compared to other ancestral species and reside at the points of the (independent) evolution of respiro-fermentation.
evidence: The results section describes the number of retained paralogs at these ancestors.

claim: The WGD ancestor and Schizosaccharomyces ancestor reside at the points of the (independent) evolution of respiro-fermentation.
source: Both ancestors also have a larger number of retained paralog pairs compared to other ancestral species and reside at the points of the (independent) evolution of respiro-fermentation.
evidence: The results section notes the association with respiro-fermentation evolution.

claim: The reassigned paralogs are enriched in carbon metabolism genes.
source: Consistently, the reassigned paralogs are enriched in carbon metabolism genes (Figure 10—source data 1).
evidence: The results section describes the functional enrichment of reassigned paralogs.

claim: Most paralogs are reassigned within a short window following their duplication.
source: Most paralogs are reassigned within a short window following their duplication.
evidence: The results section states this finding about the timing of paralog reassignment.

claim: In most cases, divergence in paralog assignment is already apparent at the immediate phylogenetic point of the duplication event.
source: In most cases, divergence in paralog assignment is already apparent at the immediate phylogenetic point of the duplication event (at the phylogenetic resolution of this study).
evidence: The results section states this finding about the timing of paralog divergence.

claim: Approximately 60% of the paralog pairs that arose at the ancestor of the Candida clade (A10) and that will eventually change their assignment, do so at that ancestor.
source: For example, ∼60% of the paralog pairs that arose at the ancestor of the Candida clade (A10) and that will eventually change their assignment, do so at that ancestor.
evidence: The results section provides a specific example of early paralog reassignment.

claim: Of all the paralog pairs that arose sporadically (not in the WGD) in the phylogeny, and where at least one member of the pair was subsequently reassigned to a different module, 53% do so 'at' the point at which they arose.
source: Overall, of all the paralog pairs that arose sporadically (not in the WGD) in the phylogeny, and where at least one member of the pair was subsequently reassigned to a different module, 53% do so 'at' the point at which they arose.
evidence: The results section reports the overall proportion of early paralog reassignment.

claim: Sporadically duplicated genes are significantly enriched among all the reassigned genes at their point of duplication, but not at later phylogenetic points.
source: Furthermore, such sporadically duplicated genes are significantly enriched (Hyper-geometric test, p<0.05,) among all the reassigned genes (duplicated or not) at their point of duplication, but not at later phylogenetic points, when they behave comparably to non-duplicated genes (Figure 10B).
evidence: The results section states this finding with statistical support.

claim: There is a short 'window of opportunity' in regulatory innovation, specifically facilitated by paralogous genes shortly after they are duplicated but not later.
source: This suggests a short 'window of opportunity' in regulatory innovation, specifically facilitated by paralogous genes shortly after they are duplicated but not later, and provides strong experimental support to previous theoretical models (Gu et al., 2005).
evidence: The results section interprets the findings about paralog reassignment timing.

claim: A similar proportion (54%) of WGD paralogs that diverge do so as early as they arise.
source: While a similar proportion (54%) of those that diverge do so as early as they arise, they continue to contribute significantly to the divergence in module assignment at later points compared to non-duplicated genes (Figure 10B, orange circles, Hyper-geometric test, p<0.05).
evidence: The results section reports the proportion of early WGD paralog reassignment.

claim: WGD paralogs continue to contribute significantly to the divergence in module assignment at later points compared to non-duplicated genes.
source: While a similar proportion (54%) of those that diverge do so as early as they arise, they continue to contribute significantly to the divergence in module assignment at later points compared to non-duplicated genes (Figure 10B, orange circles, Hyper-geometric test, p<0.05).
evidence: The results section states this finding with statistical support.

claim: The extended window of WGD paralog contribution is not simply due to the finer phylogenetic resolution in the post-WGD clade.
source: This distinction is not simply due to the finer phylogenetic resolution in the post-WGD clade in our study: the same trend is observed with eight of the 15 species with comparable resolution in the pre- and post-WGD clades (Figure 11A,B).
evidence: The results section rules out a potential confounding factor.

claim: The extended window of WGD paralog contribution may be explained by the fact that sporadically duplicated genes may not be duplicated with the full set of ancestral regulatory elements and may move to novel genomic locations.
source: This extended window may be explained by the theoretical argument (Lynch and Katju, 2004) that sporadically duplicated genes—but not WGD duplicated genes—may not be duplicated with the full set of ancestral regulatory elements and may move to novel genomic locations (Lynch and Katju, 2004), thus resulting in immediate divergence from the ancestral state.
evidence: The results section cites a theoretical explanation for the extended window.

claim: Most paralogs (66% of all pairs) have at least one member diverging from the ancestral module.
source: Most paralogs (66% of all pairs) have at least one member diverging from the ancestral module.
evidence: The results section reports the proportion of paralogs with divergence.

claim: 27% of all paralog pairs show 'classical' neo-functionalization, where one paralog maintains the ancestral assignment and the other is assigned to a different module.
source: This includes paralogs with distinct fates, either due to 'classical' neo-functionalization (27% of all pairs), where one paralog maintains the ancestral assignment and the other is assigned to a different module (e.g., the purine biosynthesis genes URA8 and URA7, Figure 10C, case 2)
evidence: The results section reports the proportion of paralogs with neo-functionalization.

claim: 12% of all paralog pairs show asymmetric divergence, where each paralog is reassigned to a distinct module, each different than the ancestral one.
source: or due to asymmetric divergence (12%), where each paralog is reassigned to a distinct module, each different than the ancestral one (e.g., the disulphide isomerases EUG1 and PDI1, Figure 10C, case 3).
evidence: The results section reports the proportion of paralogs with asymmetric divergence.

claim: 27% of all paralog pairs show symmetric divergence, where both paralogs are reassigned to the same module, distinct from the ancestral one.
source: In the remaining cases (27%) there is symmetric divergence, where both paralogs are reassigned to the same module, distinct from the ancestral one (e.g., the ribonucleotide-diphosphate reductases SER3 and SER33, Figure 10C, case 4).
evidence: The results section reports the proportion of paralogs with symmetric divergence.

claim: Only in a minority of paralog pairs (34%) the ancestral assignment of both copies is conserved.
source: Only in a minority of paralog pairs (34%) the ancestral assignment of both copies is conserved (e.g., the ribosome biogenesis genes UTP5 and UTP9, Figure 10C, case 1).
evidence: The results section reports the proportion of paralogs with conserved assignment.

claim: The 'conserved' and 'symmetrically diverged' classes could be easily confounded in previous studies relying on paralogs from a single species.
source: These classes could be easily confounded in previous studies relying on paralogs from a single species (e.g., 'conserved' and 'symmetrically diverged' would be indistinguishable).
evidence: The results section notes a limitation of prior studies.

claim: The pre-duplication orthologs of genes from the neo-functionalized class are most prominent in the 'unchanged' Module 3 and mildly induced Module 4.
source: The pre-duplication orthologs of genes from the neo-functionalized class are most prominent in the 'unchanged' Module 3 and mildly induced Module 4 (Hyper-geometric test, p<10−3), suggesting that genes that were not regulated in glucose depletion prior to duplication, 'gain' such regulation de novo post-duplication, for at least one paralog.
evidence: The results section describes the ancestral state of neo-functionalized genes.

claim: Genes that were not regulated in glucose depletion prior to duplication 'gain' such regulation de novo post-duplication, for at least one paralog.
source: The pre-duplication orthologs of genes from the neo-functionalized class are most prominent in the 'unchanged' Module 3 and mildly induced Module 4 (Hyper-geometric test, p<10−3), suggesting that genes that were not regulated in glucose depletion prior to duplication, 'gain' such regulation de novo post-duplication, for at least one paralog.
evidence: The results section interprets the ancestral state of neo-functionalized genes.

claim: Neo-functionalization has contributed to the regulatory divergence of key genes in carbon metabolism during the evolution of respiro-fermentation.
source: Neo-functionalization has also contributed to the regulatory divergence of key genes in carbon metabolism during the evolution of respiro-fermentation (Figure 8B), consistent with previous studies (Conant and Wolfe, 2007).
evidence: The results section states this finding and cites prior work.

claim: Similarity in heat stress profiles is inversely proportional to phylogenetic distance.
source: As in the response to glucose depletion, similarity in heat stress profiles is inversely proportional to phylogenetic distance (Figure 11C–F), and the strongly repressed Module 1, which consists of 'growth' genes, is the most conserved (Roy et al., 2013).
evidence: The results section compares heat shock to glucose depletion.

claim: The strongly repressed Module 1, which consists of 'growth' genes, is the most conserved in heat shock.
source: As in the response to glucose depletion, similarity in heat stress profiles is inversely proportional to phylogenetic distance (Figure 11C–F), and the strongly repressed Module 1, which consists of 'growth' genes, is the most conserved (Roy et al., 2013).
evidence: The results section compares heat shock to glucose depletion.

claim: The evolutionary trajectories of paralogous genes are highly similar between heat shock and glucose depletion.
source: Furthermore, the evolutionary trajectories of paralogous genes—including the higher reassignment of paralogs, the distinct reassignment capacity of sporadic and large-scale duplications, and the preponderance of reassignment of only one of two paralogs—are highly similar between heat shock and glucose depletion (Figure 11A,B).
evidence: The results section compares paralog trajectories between conditions.

claim: The similar patterns between heat shock and glucose depletion suggest that these are general evolutionary principles, at least in this phylogeny.
source: This suggests that these are general evolutionary principles, at least in this phylogeny.
evidence: The results section interprets the similarity between conditions.

claim: Considering both glucose depletion and heat shock responses, the conserved class of paralogs was reduced from 34% to 28%.
source: Indeed, considering both responses, the conserved class was reduced from 34% to 28%, and the majority (70%) of paralogs were in classes where either one (38%, Figure 12B,E) or both (32%, Figure 12C,E) were neo-functionalized in at least one response.
evidence: The results section reports the reclassification of paralogs when considering both conditions.

claim: The majority (70%) of paralogs were in classes where either one (38%) or both (32%) were neo-functionalized in at least one response when considering both glucose depletion and heat shock.
source: Indeed, considering both responses, the conserved class was reduced from 34% to 28%, and the majority (70%) of paralogs were in classes where either one (38%, Figure 12B,E) or both (32%, Figure 12C,E) were neo-functionalized in at least one response.
evidence: The results section reports the proportion of neo-functionalized paralogs when considering both conditions.

claim: Only 2% of all paralog pairs were in the sub-functionalized class when considering both glucose depletion and heat shock.
source: Surprisingly, only 2% of all paralog pairs were in the sub-functionalized class (Figure 12D,E).
evidence: The results section reports the low proportion of sub-functionalized paralogs.

claim: Respiro-fermentation is functionally analogous to the Warburg Effect in cancer cells.
source: Respiro-fermentation is functionally analogous to the (somatically evolved) Warburg Effect in cancer cells (Vander Heiden et al., 2009), which relies—to some extent—on the 'neo'-functionalization of metabolic enzymes.
evidence: The discussion draws an analogy between respiro-fermentation and the Warburg effect.

claim: The Warburg Effect relies—to some extent—on the 'neo'-functionalization of metabolic enzymes.
source: Respiro-fermentation is functionally analogous to the (somatically evolved) Warburg Effect in cancer cells (Vander Heiden et al., 2009), which relies—to some extent—on the 'neo'-functionalization of metabolic enzymes.
evidence: The discussion describes a mechanism of the Warburg effect.

claim: There are well-known similarities in glycolysis and respiration between respiro-fermentation and the Warburg effect.
source: There are well-known similarities in glycolysis and respiration between the two states that enable both cancer and yeast cells to direct glucose to biosynthesis, supporting their rapid growth and proliferation.
evidence: The discussion describes similarities between respiro-fermentation and the Warburg effect.

claim: Both the causes of the Warburg metabolic signature and its connection to biosynthesis are not fully understood.
source: However, both the causes of this metabolic signature and its connection to biosynthesis are not fully understood.
evidence: The discussion notes a knowledge gap about the Warburg effect.

claim: The observation that genes encoding enzymes in the nucleotide salvage and glycine biosynthesis pathways are strongly induced post-diauxic shift in respiro-fermentative post-WGD species is analogous to recently identified changes in these pathways in cancer cells that display the Warburg Effect.
source: The observation that genes encoding enzymes in the nucleotide salvage and glycine biosynthesis pathways are strongly induced post-diauxic shift in respiro-fermentative post-WGD species is analogous to recently identified changes in these pathways in cancer cells that display the Warburg Effect (Gaglio et al., 2011; Jain et al., 2012), suggests that rewiring of nucleotide biosynthetic pathways contributes to this phenotype and points to fundamental metabolic principles that are independent of evolutionary descent.
evidence: The discussion draws an analogy between yeast and cancer metabolism.

claim: Rewiring of nucleotide biosynthetic pathways contributes to the respiro-fermentative phenotype.
source: The observation that genes encoding enzymes in the nucleotide salvage and glycine biosynthesis pathways are strongly induced post-diauxic shift in respiro-fermentative post-WGD species is analogous to recently identified changes in these pathways in cancer cells that display the Warburg Effect (Gaglio et al., 2011; Jain et al., 2012), suggests that rewiring of nucleotide biosynthetic pathways contributes to this phenotype and points to fundamental metabolic principles that are independent of evolutionary descent.
evidence: The discussion interprets the findings about nucleotide biosynthesis.

claim: The findings point to fundamental metabolic principles that are independent of evolutionary descent.
source: The observation that genes encoding enzymes in the nucleotide salvage and glycine biosynthesis pathways are strongly induced post-diauxic shift in respiro-fermentative post-WGD species is analogous to recently identified changes in these pathways in cancer cells that display the Warburg Effect (Gaglio et al., 2011; Jain et al., 2012), suggests that rewiring of nucleotide biosynthetic pathways contributes to this phenotype and points to fundamental metabolic principles that are independent of evolutionary descent.
evidence: The discussion interprets the broader implications of the findings.
